name: Body language / presence training
lead: Body language or presence training is the deliberate practice of nonverbal behaviour, such as an open stance, steady eye contact, slower movements and an upright carriage, to come across as more confident, warm and commanding. In appearance communities it is treated as the part of looks that moves: two people with the same face can leave different impressions depending on how they hold and present themselves.[1][2]

Wikipedia defines body language as nonverbal communication through posture, gestures, facial expressions, eye movement, touch and use of space, mostly occurring without conscious awareness, and notes that open, relaxed postures and a forward chest are linked to impressions of confidence and trust.[1] On looksmax.org, members write guides on 'charismamaxxing' that pair body language with voice tone and humour, and threads on reading interest and indifference in others.[3][4]
Research on trained postures is mixed. The power-posing literature found a reliable effect on how people feel but no reliable effect on hormones, and an unclear effect on behaviour.[5]

chain: Practise open posture, eye contact and calm movement
Others read more confidence and warmth
Stronger first impression and social presence
angle.text: Practitioners use body language training to change the impression their appearance gives, standing taller, holding eye contact and moving more slowly so that their looks are read alongside confidence. The practice costs nothing and is done alongside posture work, grooming and style.

paras: The study of body movement in communication is called kinesics. Ray Birdwhistell, who developed it, held that gestures are polysemic and cannot be decoded in any absolute way, and rejected the term "body language".[1] Edward T. Hall introduced proxemics in 1966, defining intimate, personal, social and public distance zones.[1]

Reports note that leaning forward and nodding suggests openness, folded arms are often read as a closed mind, and relaxed hands suggest confidence.[1] Firm handshakes are said to improve the accuracy of first impressions.[1] Eye contact is often read as sincerity in workplaces, but meaning varies by culture, with prolonged gaze seen as a challenge or anger in some cultures.[1] The same gesture can differ in meaning: arms akimbo may signal relaxed confidence in Western countries but is considered rude in Bali.[1]
A family-medicine review on cross-cultural care lists attitudes toward personal space, eye contact and body language among the areas where expectations differ between cultures.[6]

In 2010 Dana Carney, Amy Cuddy and Andy Yap reported that holding expansive poses changed hormone levels in 42 participants, and Cuddy popularised the idea in a 2012 TED talk.[5] A 2015 replication by Eva Ranehill and colleagues found an effect on felt power but not on hormones, risk tolerance or behaviour.[5] Carney stated in 2016 that she no longer believed the effect was real, while Cuddy and colleagues published a 2018 meta-analysis of 55 studies reporting evidential value for effects on feelings.[5] A 2022 meta-analysis of 128 studies reported reliable effects on thoughts and feelings, no effect on physiological measures and an unclear behavioural effect, with few studies including a neutral-posture control.[5]

A looksmax.org guide to charismamaxxing argues that charisma can make a difference to dating, jobs and friendships even for tall, conventionally attractive men, and splits it into body language, voice tonality and humour.[4] It cites the 7%-38%-55% split attributed to Mehrabian, a figure Wikipedia notes is widely debated.[1][4]

Another thread, by a member who says he has studied body language for months, lists signs he associates with interest, such as preening, frequent eye contact and nervous behaviour, while noting that no single sign is conclusive.[3] Further threads on the forum cover mirroring body language and social-skills guides.[7][8]

Scholars disagree whether body language is universal, and Mehrabian's often-cited 7%-38%-55% split is widely debated.[1] Wikipedia states there is no scientific evidence that nonverbal cues reliably detect lies.[1] A 2021 BJPsych International review observed that people may be less skilled at reading others' faces and body language than they think.[9]
No studies found for presence training as a looks-related intervention. Related laboratory research on power posing is summarised above.[5]

lore.intro: Body language is discussed on looksmax.org as part of 'charisma' and social skills, often alongside voice and humour, with members sharing guides on how to project confidence and read others.[3][4]

claims.claim: Body language and tone carry most of the meaning in communication
claims.believers: A charisma guide on looksmax.org states that 7% of communication is words, 38% tone and 55% body language.[4]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that Mehrabian's percentages remain widely debated and that the study of kinesics holds gestures cannot be decoded in any absolute way.[1]

claims.claim: Consistent signs in someone's body language reveal interest or indifference
claims.believers: One forum author lists preening, frequent eye contact and nervous behaviour as signs of attraction, advising that context matters.[3]
claims.experts: A 2021 review notes people may be worse at reading others' body language than they assume, and Wikipedia says nonverbal cues have no scientific support as reliable lie detectors.[1][9]

claims.claim: Expansive poses make you feel and act more powerful
claims.believers: Power-posing advocates, led by Amy Cuddy, argue that posing can make people feel more powerful.[5]
claims.experts: A 2022 meta-analysis of 128 studies found reliable effects on thoughts and feelings but none on physiological measures, with behavioural effects unclear.[5]

card.summary: Training stance, eye contact and pace to look more confident; the research supports felt confidence more than outcomes.
card.note: Meanings of gestures vary by culture; power-posing hormone effects were not replicated.

quick.overview:
Body language training means practising open posture, steady eye contact and calmer movement to project confidence.

Power-posing research found reliable effects on how people feel, but not on hormones, and behavioural effects are unclear. Gesture meanings also vary across cultures.
quick.mechanism: Practitioners say changing outward behaviour alters how others read confidence and may feed back into mood. Studies support the mood link more than the others.
quick.risks: Low risk. Cross-cultural misreading of gestures and eye contact is the main caveat noted in references.
